The Dual Enterprise: The Work and Teaching of Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud (the First Raavad)
Guide to the Source
This report surveys the work of Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud, the First Raavad, and describes him as a bridging figure who sought to defend Rabbinic Judaism in the 12th century against intellectual and political threats. The text clarifies his uniqueness as the father of Aristotelian rationalism in Judaism, while distinguishing him from other sages bearing the same title, and analyses his "dual enterprise": fortifying the historical authority of the tradition of the Sages through "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" against the Karaites, and establishing the rationality of faith in his philosophical work "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah". Through a survey of his life and an analysis of his thought, the source presents the Raavad as a pioneer who paved the way for Maimonides (Rambam) by combining the natural sciences with theology, while maintaining a "limited rationalism" that recognises the supremacy of faith where human reason comes to a halt. Ultimately, the work emerges as a unified apologetic whole intended to prove that Torah and wisdom do not contradict each other but complement each other.
The Dual Enterprise: The Work and Teaching of Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud (the First Raavad)
Executive Summary
This report presents a comprehensive analysis of the work and teaching of Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud HaLevi (the First Raavad, 1110–1180). He is placed as a key intellectual figure of the 12th century who identified a twofold threat to Rabbinic Judaism: an internal threat from Karaism, which undermined the authority of the Oral Torah, and an external threat from the rationalist challenge of Aristotelian philosophy and the political pressures of a changing world.
In response, the First Raavad developed a two-pronged defensive enterprise. The first axis, expressed in his historiographical work "Sefer ha-Kabbalah", was intended to fortify the historical authority and continuity of the oral tradition. The second axis, expressed in his philosophical work "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah", established for the first time in Jewish thought the rationality of faith on systematic Aristotelian foundations. This report will analyse these two axes not as separate works but as a single intellectual whole, apologetic and coherent, intended to defend Rabbinic Judaism and prepare it for the challenges of medieval modernity.
Introduction: Identification and Clarification – the First Raavad in His Proper Place
Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud HaLevi (the First Raavad) was a Spanish polymath – philosopher, historian and astronomer – who lived and worked at the height of the Golden Age in Spain, but also at a time of deep existential crisis.[1, 2] His work represents a critical juncture in Jewish thought, at which the defence of tradition encountered Aristotelian philosophy systematically for the first time.
A critical necessity at the outset of the discussion is to resolve the semantic confusion surrounding the title "the Raavad". This confusion is not merely technical; it blurs opposing poles in the history of Jewish thought. The title "the Raavad" is used for at least three major figures, the two most famous of whom – the first and the third – represent opposite worldviews. The First Raavad, Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud, is the founding father of Aristotelian rationalism in Judaism.[3] In contrast, the Third Raavad, Rabbi Avraham ben David of Posquières, is the sharpest critic of rationalism (in the form of his critical glosses on Maimonides) and the defender of mysticism and of the Provençal tradition.[4, 5]
To set the discussion on firm ground, the following table clarifies the essential distinctions:
Table 1: Distinguishing Between the Three "Raavads"
This report will focus exclusively on the First Raavad. The central thesis to be presented is that the First Raavad identified in the 12th century a twofold threat to Rabbinic Judaism: a threat from within (the Karaites' challenge to the authority of the tradition) and a threat from without (the challenge of philosophy and political persecution). In response, he created a two-pronged defensive enterprise: "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" fortified the historical authority of the tradition, and "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" established its philosophical rationality. The two works are not separate creations, but a single, calculated apologetic whole.
Chapter 1: The Man and His Times – Between the Muslim Hammer and the Christian Anvil
Biography and the Formative Trauma
Rabbi Avraham ibn Daud was born in Córdoba, in Muslim Spain, around the year 1110.[1, 6] He was the scion of a distinguished family, the grandson of the scholar Rabbenu Yitzhak ben Albalia.[1] His life unfolded at the heart of the intellectual centre of the Golden Age, but this period came to its violent end with the rise of the Almohad dynasty (al-Muwahhidun).
The Almohads were a zealous Muslim religious movement that conquered North Africa and southern Spain, including Córdoba. They abolished the "Pact of Umar", which had allowed Jews and Christians to exist as protected subjects ("dhimmi"), and set before the Jews an unequivocal choice: conversion to Islam, death or expulsion. This trauma is the formative event in the life of the First Raavad. He fled for his life from Córdoba and found refuge in Toledo, which was now under Christian rule.[1]
The flight from the trauma of the Almohads' religious persecutions profoundly shaped his historiographical outlook. His writing is not coolly academic but a passionate theological response to the events of his time. In "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" he analyses history in terms of divine reward and punishment taking place in real time.[7] He praises in exceptional terms Alfonso VII, the Christian king of Castile who received the Jewish refugees in Toledo, calling him "king of kings" and "a righteous king".[7] He sees Alfonso's rise and his military success against the Muslims as a positive divine recompense for his tolerance, and as a direct punishment of the intolerant Almohads.[7] In this way, his historiography becomes a tool for understanding divine justice in the politics of his time.
His Work in Toledo and His Tragic End
In Toledo, which had become a vibrant cultural centre of interreligious encounter, the First Raavad found fertile ground for his activity. He was versed in every branch of wisdom and science, and is mentioned in the sources as an astronomer, in addition to being a philosopher and historian.[1, 2]
The end of the First Raavad is shrouded in a certain mist, but the main tradition, which appears among other places in "Shevet Yehuda", holds that he died a martyr's death (al kiddush Hashem) in Toledo in the year 1180.[1, 5, 6] According to the account, the king of Spain (apparently Alfonso's successor) tried to force him to convert. The Raavad refused, "sanctified the Name in public", and was executed.[1]
There is a deep tragic irony in the course of his life. He fled the persecutions of the extremist Muslims (the Almohads) and found safe refuge with the Christian king whom he had extolled as "a righteous king".[7] Yet in the end he met his death as a martyr precisely under Christian rule, in his city of refuge, Toledo.[1] This symbolises the existential fragility of the Jewish communities in medieval Spain, and the constant movement between patronage and deadly persecution in both worlds, the Muslim and the Christian.
Chapter 2: "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" – Shaping History as a Polemical Act
Historiography as Defence: Establishing the Chain of Tradition
The Raavad's first major work, "Sefer ha-Kabbalah", is not a mere historical chronicle, but a foundational text of Jewish historical consciousness, whose chief purpose is apologetic and polemical.[1, 8] The Raavad states his intentions clearly in his introduction: "We wrote it to inform the students that all the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory, the sages of the Mishnah and the Talmud, are all received tradition".[8]
The central claim of the book is that the Oral Torah, in all its components (Mishnah and Talmud), was transmitted in a continuous, meticulous and unbroken chain, "from mouth to mouth", from Moses our teacher down to the sages of his own time, such as the Ri Migash and the Raavad's teacher, R. Baruch Albalia.[1, 8] His aim is to prove that the Talmud "spread throughout all Israel and they accepted it... and to it nothing may be added and from it nothing may be taken away".[8]
The Polemic Against the Karaites: History as an Instrument of Dispossession
The direct enemy from within, against whom the work is directed, is Karaite Judaism.[1, 8] The strategy the Raavad adopts against them is not primarily theological and exegetical (as Rasag had done), but historiographical.
The Karaites claimed that Rabbinic Judaism was a late innovation that had deviated from pure Scripture. The Raavad understood that to defeat this claim, exegetical debate was not enough; he had to prove that Rabbinic Judaism alone possessed continuous historical legitimacy. "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" builds a meticulous historical narrative of transmission, emphasising the authority passed from generation to generation. As a result, any group that is not within this golden chain (that is, the Karaites) is automatically presented as a deviation, a late innovation, a secession and something "invented out of his own heart".[9] "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" thus uses history as a tool to dispossess the Karaites of all historical legitimacy.
At this point, the comparison with the approach of Maimonides, his younger contemporary, is instructive.[9] Maimonides, in his Commentary on the Mishnah (Avot 1:3), attributes the origin of the deviation to Zadok and Boethus, disciples of Antigonus of Sokho, who acted out of an ancient theological error (a mistaken understanding of the idea of reward and punishment). By contrast, the Raavad in "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" attributes the origin of the deviation (or at least its renewal and strengthening) to the figure of Anan ben David, who was active in the period of the Geonim. The Raavad ascribes Anan's secession not to a purely theological motive, but to personal and political motives: "a grudge [jealousy] that was in his heart" after he was not appointed Exilarch, and therefore "he rose to lead Israel astray from the tradition of the Sages".[9]
The difference between the approaches is significant: Maimonides sees Karaism as an ancient ideological heresy. The Raavad presents it as a late historical deviation that arose from internal politics. Thus the Raavad's approach turns Karaism into a concrete historical event that can be pointed to as a "secession" from the authentic mainstream, and in this way it is more effective as a polemical-historical tool.
The Appendices: Extending the Polemic Against Christianity
The Raavad's polemic is not limited to the Karaites alone. As one who lived and worked in Christian Toledo, he recognised that Christianity too challenges the historical legitimacy of Rabbinic Judaism. The two appendices to "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" were intended to deal with this second front.[8]
"The History of the Kings of Israel in the Second Temple Period": this work, based on "Sefer Yosippon and other books", was explicitly intended "to prove the truth of the coming of the Messiah and to refute the doctrine of the Karaites and the Christians".[8]
"Zikhron Divrei Romi" (A Record of the Affairs of Rome): this work deals with the history of Rome, and its aim is "to prove the position of the sages of Israel concerning the birth of Jesus the Nazarene, and more".[8]
Through these appendices, the Raavad extends his historiographical enterprise. He uses history to undermine the chronological and messianic narrative of Christianity, just as he used it to undermine the legitimacy of Karaism.
Chapter 3: "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" – The Founding of Jewish Aristotelianism
Innovation and Primacy: The Philosophical Revolution
If "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" was the historical front, "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" (in the Arabic original: "al-Aqida al-Rafi'a" – 'The Exalted Faith') was the philosophical front.[3, 10] This work is recognised in scholarship as "the first Jewish Aristotelian work".[3, 10]
Its status as "the first" is critical. The Raavad worked before Maimonides, and in fact paved the way for him. The Jewish philosophy that preceded him, such as that of Rasag, was based mainly on the school of the "Kalam" (Muslim speculative theology). Aristotelianism, as developed by Muslim philosophers such as Ibn Sina and Ibn Bajja, posed a new challenge, systematic and far more persuasive. The Raavad was the first who dared to confront this challenge head-on, not by rejecting it, but by adopting it and "converting" it. He sought to prove that one can "hold two lamps in one's two hands", as he describes it: "in his right hand the fire of religion and in his left the lamp of his wisdom".[1] "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" is the first systematic attempt to light these two lamps together, and to show that the Jewish faith accords with Aristotelian philosophy.[1]
The Arabic original of the work was lost, but it was preserved in two medieval Hebrew translations [3, 10]: the first, the translation of Shlomo ibn Labi, called "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah", and the second, the translation of Shmuel Motot, called "Ha-Emunah ha-Nissa'ah".[10]
The Structure of the Work as a Philosophical Argument
The structure of the book, divided into three "treatises" (parts), is in itself a radical philosophical argument.[1, 11]
First Treatise: The Physical Foundation ("On Natural Science and What Comes After It") The Raavad opens not with quotations from the Torah, but with a purely Aristotelian discussion of basic concepts in physics and metaphysics: substance and accident, matter and form, the kinds of accidents, and so on.[1, 11] This order is revolutionary. The Raavad in effect establishes that the Jewish reader must study the foundations of Aristotelian science and metaphysics before he can properly approach a rational understanding of God and of faith. Philosophy becomes the necessary gateway to theology.
Second Treatise: The Theological Foundation (the Principles of Religion) Only after establishing the philosophical infrastructure does the Raavad move on to discuss matters of religion and faith. This treatise presents six "principles" or "roots" of faith, and in it he applies the Aristotelian tools of the first treatise to central theological questions.[1, 11]
Third Treatise: The Ethical Foundation ("On the Healing of the Soul") The work concludes with an ethical discussion of the qualities of the soul and its healing.[1, 11] In this way, the Raavad connects the entire course of the argument back to its practical purpose. He argues that the ultimate goal of the philosophical (First Treatise) and theological (Second Treatise) enterprise is to bring a person to the refinement of character and to an ethical life (Third Treatise), which are themselves the supreme aim of the Torah. With this argument he closes the circle and establishes that "everything philosophy has dealt with is already found in the Torah".[1]
Chapter 4: A Theological Analysis of "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" (the Second Treatise)
The core of the First Raavad's theology is presented in the second treatise of "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah". This treatise is built around six principles (or roots) [1, 11]:
The root of faith: the existence of God (a proof by means of the Aristotelian concept of the "Prime Mover").
The unity of God: the negation of corporeality and multiplicity.
The attributes of God: a discussion of the attributes of action and the negation of essential attributes (a move that anticipates the approach of Maimonides).
The actions of God (prophecy): the presentation of prophecy as a rational-intellectual process influenced by God.
Individual providence.
Free will.
Out of this whole, two key questions illustrate the Raavad's distinctive method and the limits of his Aristotelianism.
Creation Versus the Eternity of the World
Aristotelian philosophy, as understood in the Middle Ages, claimed the eternal pre-existence of the world, in contradiction to the Jewish principle of faith of creation "ex nihilo". Here we witness the first breaking point, at which the Raavad sets a clear limit to philosophy. He firmly defends the principle of creation "ex nihilo", and rejects the claim of eternity. Moreover, he states explicitly: "And likewise we are not to speculate about creation, that it is something from nothing".[1] This is an important statement: the Raavad is a rationalist, but not a total rationalist. When a philosophical conclusion (eternity) contradicts an absolute principle of faith (creation), he rejects philosophy and sets a restriction on further rational inquiry into the matter.
The Great Paradox: Divine Knowledge and Free Will
The most complex and most famous question in his teaching is the attempt to reconcile God's absolute knowledge (knowledge of future events) with man's free will.[1] This is the core problem of ethical responsibility, which is the foundation of the entire Torah.
The Raavad formulates the problem in all its sharpness, but his solution is not philosophical-rational, but in a certain sense anti-philosophical.[1] First, he sharply attacks anyone who tries to resolve the contradiction by simplistic rational means: "One who raises this difficulty... is a complete fool, and why should he involve himself in such doubts and considerations".[1] Second, he presents a fideistic (faith-based) solution that recognises the limitations of human reason: "Rather, the answer is: who can fathom the secrets of the Most High".[1] Third, he establishes that divine knowledge is not of the same kind as human understanding ("for His knowledge is not like our understanding"), and therefore, although God knows, "we are not compelled".[1] Finally, he arrives at the conclusion that both principles (knowledge and choice) must be accepted as true, even if the connection between them is hidden from us, and therefore one must "leave this matter to God".[1]
This is a decisive point. The Raavad uses sharp philosophical tools to formulate the problem as precisely as possible, and then, instead of solving it philosophically (as Maimonides would attempt in the "Guide of the Perplexed"), he establishes that the solution lies beyond the capacity of human reason. He is a philosopher who recognises the limitations of philosophy, and prefers to accept a paradox of faith rather than give up one of its two foundations (divine knowledge or human choice).
Chapter 5: Synthesis and Legacy – Between "Correspondence" and "Fusion"
One Teaching, Two Faces: The Dual Enterprise
When one examines the whole of the First Raavad's work, a single defensive enterprise emerges, with two complementary faces. "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" and "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" are not two separate books dealing with different subjects, but two parts of the same apologetic strategy.
"Sefer ha-Kabbalah" fortified the historical authority of the Oral Torah. It met the Karaite challenge and provided an answer to the question: "From whom did we receive it?".
"Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah" fortified the rational authority of the Oral Torah. It met the challenge of Aristotelian philosophy and provided an answer to the question: "Is what we received reasonable?".
Together, the two works created a comprehensive defence of Rabbinic Judaism, both inwardly (against the Karaites) and outwardly (against Christianity and philosophy).
The Forerunner and the Heir: The First Raavad and Maimonides
It is impossible to understand the enterprise of Maimonides without knowing the First Raavad, who preceded him. The First Raavad was the forerunner and the pioneer who paved the way for the Jewish Aristotelian project. Nevertheless, there is an essential difference in their methods.[12]
The First Raavad carried out "parallelism and correspondence".[12] He placed the lamp of Torah and the lamp of wisdom side by side.[1] He showed that they do not contradict each other, but did not always fuse them completely. As we have seen, when a head-on contradiction emerged (in creation or in free will), he preferred the Torah and recognised the limitations of reason.[1]
Maimonides, by contrast, aspired to a "new fusion" and a systematic and total synthesis.[12] Maimonides would try to show that the Torah is philosophy at its best, and that philosophy is the only way to understand the Torah. He would try to resolve the paradox of knowledge and choice by rational means, and would not be content with the statement that this is a "supreme secret".
Conclusion: The Independent Importance of the First Raavad
The legacy of the First Raavad goes beyond his being merely "the forerunner of Maimonides". He is a great and important thinker in his own right. He was the pioneer who dared to confront the Aristotelian challenge directly and systematically. His "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" became a cornerstone of Jewish historiography, and all the later chronicles (such as "Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah") relied on it directly.[1]
In "Ha-Emunah ha-Ramah", he established a distinctive model of "limited rationalism" – maximal use of reason, together with an honest and courageous recognition of its limitations in the face of the principles of faith. In this way, he offered a model different from that of Maimonides, and perhaps no less sustainable, for the eternal balance between faith and reason. His dual work reshaped the defence of Rabbinic Judaism and prepared the ground for the 12th century to establish itself as the peak of Jewish thought in the Middle Ages.
